claims.text: Compositionally complex or high-entropy alloy systems can be used to produce a ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
Resistance to temper embrittlement enables the proposed ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
The relevant transition can be induced through systematic temperature variation.
The proposed behavior occurs within a narrow temperature window.
Atomic structure and composition mediate the response to temperature variation.
Temper-embrittlement mechanisms are suppressed in compositionally complex or high-entropy alloy systems.
Compositionally complex or high-entropy alloy systems will undergo a ductile–brittle–ductile transition without a dramatic loss of ductility.
Temper embrittlement in conventional alloys occurs over a bounded temperature range.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes a ductile–brittle–ductile transition to suppression of temper embrittlement, but it does not identify another mechanism that would produce the intervening brittle state. The predicted transition is also described as occurring without dramatic ductility loss, which conflicts conceptually with an asserted brittle regime unless brittleness is defined by another measured property.
